rationale: A wins because it turns missing facts into gates instead of decoration. A's line, "Partial disclosure kills this angle," is exactly the discipline this launch needs; B's "brand known for $20 chargers" and "competing on price the way it did in chargers" wanders outside the brief. B has usable bones, but A is the set I would let near a founder before a reporter call.
gaps_in_A: "purchase costing thousands of dollars and living on the side of the house for a decade" imports price and longevity assumptions the update did not give; say high-consideration home infrastructure until pricing and warranty terms are nailed down.

"The prevailing belief is that whole-home batteries mean panel work, transfer switches, and an electrician's week" may be true, but it is outside the supplied facts; frame it as what installers will test, not as established beat consensus.

"A profitable charger maker bets on a capital-heavy market" is useful but thin; A admits it "should not be pitched until at least one financial detail exists," so it belongs below the three ready shapes.
gaps_in_B: "brand known for $20 chargers" and "purchase measured in thousands of dollars and decades on the wall" decorate the facts with numbers and lifespan claims the update did not provide.
"category-creation" is the wrong label. Tesla Powerwall already defines the category in the brief, so this is brand-extension strategy, not category creation.
"competing on price the way it did in chargers" invents Anker's historical price positioning and turns partially disclosed pricing into a thesis.
"cash-hungry energy business" is not in the update; calling that refused angle only a duplicate misses the unsupported claim and throws away a potentially valid financial-risk lens.
